analysis.body:
# AI Data Center Energy Demand: A Grid Operator View

Across five major US grid operators, 8,380 generation and storage projects totaling 1.33 million MW are in interconnection queues as of mid-September 2026. This represents generation waiting to connect, not data center demand itself, but the fuel mix tells a story relevant to AI workload growth: storage capacity alone accounts for 326.7 thousand MW, while natural gas projects total 184.5 thousand MW. Solar dominates the mix at 429.7 thousand MW. The distribution is uneven: ERCOT's Texas queue holds 438 thousand MW across 1,778 requests, while CAISO's California queue, despite being a primary data center hub, contains only 71.7 thousand MW across 265 requests—a reflection of California's existing transmission constraints and interconnection challenges.

Commercial electricity sales across eight states reached 54.8 thousand GWh in the second quarter of 2026, a proxy for data center load since data centers are billed as commercial customers. Texas led absolute consumption at 15.75 thousand GWh, followed by California at 10.02 thousand GWh, though California's price per MWh ($27.33) was more than triple Texas's ($8.66). Virginia, Illinois, and Ohio each recorded between 5.5 and 7.8 thousand GWh. These price differentials matter: lower-cost electricity in Texas and the Southwest Power Pool region correlates with both queue depth and developer interest, while California's high prices reflect both demand and supply constraints.

The relationship between queue depth and electricity pricing suggests developers are routing new capacity toward cheaper regions. ERCOT and SPP, serving low-cost areas, host proportionally larger queues relative to current commercial load, while CAISO's constrained queue reflects the cost of entry and transmission bottlenecks. Storage projects clustered in ERCOT (159.8 thousand MW) and SPP (52.9 thousand MW) suggest that grid operators and developers expect volatility in peak demand, likely driven by clustered data center expansion. Watch whether CAISO's queue begins growing faster than its transmission constraints expand, as this would signal whether high-cost California can retain AI workload or whether cost arbitrage drives buildout elsewhere.
